Appendix: Model Objects and Cohort Guarantees

Source: vignettes/model-objects.Rmd
model-objects.Rmd

A mystery-caller analysis can execute without error and still be wrong. The model converges, the incidence rate ratio looks plausible, the paragraph generator produces a sentence — and the denominator in that sentence is not the number of calls the model was fitted on. This appendix documents the structure of a fitted model object, the accessors it answers, and the invariants the fitters enforce to make that particular failure impossible rather than merely unlikely.

1. What a fitted object contains

mysterycall_poisson_model() and mysterycall_nb_model() return a classed list. The elements a reader is most likely to want:

Element What it holds
model The underlying glmerMod or glmmTMB fit, untouched
irr_table One row per fixed effect: estimate, SE, z, p, IRR, CI bounds
n Rows the model was fitted on
n_dropped Rows the complete-case filter removed, with the reason
n_clusters Distinct values of the random-intercept grouping variable
conf_level The confidence level the intervals were computed at
factor_refs Reference level chosen for each factor predictor
formula The formula passed to the engine, including the offset term
overdispersion Pearson dispersion statistic (a single number)
dispersion_details How that statistic was computed (see section 4)
convergence converged, singular, and the diagnostic messages
fit_warnings Engine warnings, de-duplicated
aic, bic Information criteria

mysterycall_lmm() stores coef_table and gmr_table instead of irr_table; mysterycall_logistic_model() stores or_table. Everything else is the same.

2. Standard accessors

All four fitted-model classes answer the usual accessors, so they can be handled like any other fitted model. Each delegates to the engine rather than recomputing anything.

coef(fit)       # fixed effects on the link scale
vcov(fit)       # fixed-effect covariance, as a base matrix
confint(fit)    # Wald intervals, at the level the model was fitted with
nobs(fit)       # rows the engine fitted
formula(fit)
fitted(fit)     # conditional on the estimated random effects
residuals(fit)  # type = "pearson" available
summary(fit)    # classed mysterycall_model_summary, with a print method

Three details are worth knowing.

coef() returns fixed effects, not the random-effect matrix. stats::coef() on a merMod returns one row per group. These methods return lme4::fixef() — or the conditional component of glmmTMB::fixef() — so exp(coef(fit)) reproduces fit$irr_table$irr.

confint() cannot disagree with the table. It defaults to the conf_level the model was fitted with rather than a hard-coded 0.95, so a model fitted at 90% reports a 90% interval. For mysterycall_lmm() it uses the Satterthwaite tt quantile with the per-term degrees of freedom, matching fit$coef_table; a normal quantile would be anticonservative at small residual df. These are Wald intervals — not profile-likelihood, not bootstrap. For a profile interval, call confint(fit$model, method = "profile") on the engine fit directly.

fitted() is conditional, not marginal. It includes the estimated random effects. For population-average predictions over a covariate profile, use mysterycall_predicted_means() or mysterycall_marginal_effects().

These methods exist only for the four classes that wrap a real fit. The table and report classes are formatted results, not models, and do not answer them. An object whose $model element has been removed raises an explicit error rather than returning NULL.

3. The analytic-cohort invariant

This is the part that protects a published denominator.

A fitting engine applies its own na.action to the model frame. A value that is fine in the data but becomes undefined inside the formula is therefore dropped by the engine, without ever passing through the package’s complete-case filter. The clearest case is a log offset:

# exposure contains three negative values
calls$exposure[1:3] <- -1

fit <- mysterycall_poisson_model(
  calls, "wait_days", "insurance", "npi", offset_col = "exposure"
)

offset(log(exposure)) is NaN for those rows. lme4 silently drops them, fits on 117 rows, and the object used to report n = 120, n_dropped = 0. Nothing in the output said otherwise, and every rate, percentage and denominator downstream was wrong by three.

Two guarantees now stand between that data and a result.

Exposure is validated before fitting. A column used as a log offset must be strictly positive and finite. The error names the column, how many values fail, the offending values, and the rows in your data frame:

#> Error: `exposure` (offset_col) must be strictly positive and finite to be
#> used as log(exposure); 3 of 120 value(s) are not, including -1, -1, -1 at
#> row(s) 1, 2, 3. Zero or negative exposure is not replaced with a small
#> constant: drop or correct those rows explicitly.

Those rows are not quietly repaired. Substituting a small positive constant for a zero exposure is a study-specific decision with consequences for the estimand, and it belongs to the analyst.

The fitted cohort is reconciled against the reported one. After fitting, every fitter that reports an n — mysterycall_poisson_model(), mysterycall_nb_model(), mysterycall_lmm(), mysterycall_logistic_model() and mysterycall_gee() — compares the rows the engine used against the complete-case count and refuses to return a mismatch:

#> Error: mysterycall_poisson_model(): the fitted model used 117 row(s) but
#> 120 complete case(s) were supplied. The fitting engine dropped 3 row(s) on
#> its own, so the reported cohort would not match the model.

So fit$n is the number the model used, and fit$n + fit$n_dropped is the number you supplied. A legitimate exclusion still happens through the documented route — the complete-case filter — which counts it and messages the count.

For the same reason, subset and na.action are refused when passed through .... Both would make the engine fit a different set of rows than the function reports. Filter the data before calling instead, so the exclusion is visible and counted.

Missing, undefined, and invalid

The three are not the same thing, and are handled differently on purpose.

Value Treatment Why
NA Dropped, counted in n_dropped A declared missing observation
NaN Refused Would otherwise pass as declared missingness
Inf Refused Not a finite count or exposure
Negative count Refused Outside the support of the distribution
Fractional Warned; refused under strict_counts = TRUE See below

NaN is refused rather than dropped because is.na(NaN) is TRUE: left alone it would be counted as a declared missing observation, when it is actually the residue of an invalid computation that nobody declared.

A fractional outcome is ambiguous rather than wrong. A count of days until an appointment is integer-valued by construction, so a fractional value is a data error. Elapsed time measured in days may legitimately carry decimals — but then a count distribution is the wrong model for it, and a continuous-time model should be considered. The default warns; strict_counts = TRUE refuses the fit. Values are never rounded or truncated under either setting.

4. Convergence, singularity, and dispersion

convergence$converged reports the optimizer — and the Hessian, for glmmTMB. It is not cleared by a warning about something else, such as a non-integer outcome.

convergence$singular is reported separately, because a boundary-singular random-effect variance is a property of the data rather than an optimizer failure. A singular fit whose optimizer returned code 0 has converged. This matters in mystery-caller designs, where a physician called only two or three times often supports no estimable random intercept.

Every captured engine warning is in fit_warnings. Convergence-related warnings are never discarded, however many unrelated ones fired.

overdispersion is a single number; dispersion_details records how it was reached, so a reader can reproduce it:

str(fit$dispersion_details)
#> List of 9
#>  $ method       : chr "Pearson chi-square / (n - p_fixed)"
#>  $ formula      : chr "sum(residuals(model, type = 'pearson')^2) / ..."
#>  $ pearson_chisq: num 207
#>  $ df           : int 192
#>  $ n            : int 196
#>  $ n_parameters : int 4
#>  $ df_engine    : num 191
#>  $ assumptions  : chr "Approximate diagnostic. ..."
#>  $ n_pearson_na : int 0

pearson_chisq / df equals overdispersion exactly. Two denominator conventions are in circulation: this one debits the fixed-effect parameters, while stats::df.residual() also debits the random-effect variance components and is therefore smaller by one for a single random intercept. df_engine records the latter so the difference is visible rather than implicit. The statistic is approximate for a GLMM in any case — its reference chi-square distribution is asymptotic and does not hold exactly once random effects are estimated.

The residuals come from the fitting engine, so the variance function matches the model as fitted. That matters when a ziformula or dispformula is supplied through ...: a hand-written NB2 variance would be the wrong denominator for a zero-inflated fit, because the fitted values are then the zero-inflation-marginal mean.

5. What to check before reporting 

fit$n                      # the denominator to report
fit$n_dropped              # exclusions, and the message said why
fit$n + fit$n_dropped      # should equal nrow(your_data)
fit$convergence$converged  # optimizer
fit$convergence$singular   # data, not failure
fit$overdispersion         # with dispersion_details to back it
fit$factor_refs            # the comparison your IRRs are against
fit$conf_level             # the level your intervals are at

mysterycall_strobe_checklist(model_result = fit) reads most of these and reports which items a methods section still needs.
